paragraphs: “I wouldn’t tell him that for anything,” said Alyosha with a smile.
“Ech! You think it hurts him? Not a bit. He’s jealous on purpose. He couldn’t care less,” Grushenka said bitterly.
“On purpose?” Alyosha asked.

“You’re silly, Alyosha, I tell you. For all your cleverness you understand nothing about this. It doesn’t offend me that he’s jealous of a girl like me. What would offend me is if he weren’t jealous. That’s the way I am. Jealousy doesn’t insult me. I have a fierce heart too, and I can be jealous myself. What does offend me is that he doesn’t love me at all. I tell you, he’s jealous now _on purpose_. Do you think I’m blind? Can’t I see? Just now he started on about that woman, about Katerina. She was this, she was that, she’d ordered a doctor from Moscow to try to save him, she’d ordered the best lawyer, the most learned one too. So he loves her, if he’ll sing her praises to my face. Shame on him! He’s treated me badly himself, so he went for me first, to make me the guilty one and put it all on me. ‘You were with your Pole before me, so I can’t be blamed over Katerina.’ That’s what it all comes to. He wants to dump the whole blame on me. He picked a quarrel on purpose, on purpose, I tell you, but I’ll—”
Grushenka never got to say what she would do. She hid her eyes in her handkerchief and broke into violent sobs.
“He doesn’t love Katerina Ivanovna,” Alyosha said firmly.

“Well, whether he loves her or not, I’ll find out soon enough,” said Grushenka, her voice turning threatening as she took the handkerchief from her eyes. Her face was twisted. Alyosha saw with sorrow that it had changed from mild and calm to sullen and spiteful.

“Enough of this nonsense,” she said suddenly. “That’s not what I sent for you about. Alyosha, darling, tomorrow—what is going to happen tomorrow? That’s what eats at me! And it eats at no one but me! I look around, and nobody is thinking about it. Nobody cares. Do you even think about it? Tomorrow he’s going on trial, you know. Tell me, how will they try him? You know it was the valet, the valet who killed him! Good heavens! Could they convict him in the valet’s place, with nobody to speak up for him? They haven’t bothered the valet at all, have they?”

“They questioned him hard,” Alyosha said thoughtfully, “but everyone came to the conclusion that it wasn’t him. He’s lying very sick now. He’s been ill ever since that fit. Really ill,” Alyosha added.
“Oh, dear! Couldn’t you go to that lawyer yourself and tell him the whole thing? They say he was brought down from Petersburg for three thousand roubles.”

“The three thousand came from the three of us together—Ivan, Katerina Ivanovna and me—but she paid the two thousand for the Moscow doctor herself. Fetyukovitch would have charged more, but the case is known all over Russia now. It’s discussed in every paper and journal. Fetyukovitch agreed to come mostly for the glory of it, since the case has become so notorious. I saw him yesterday.”
“Well? Did you speak to him?” Grushenka put in eagerly.
“He listened and said nothing. He told me he had already made up his mind. But he promised to give what I said some thought.”
“Some thought! Ah, they’re swindlers! They’ll be the ruin of him. And why did she send for the doctor?”
“As an expert witness. They want to prove that Mitya is insane and that he committed the murder without knowing what he was doing.” Alyosha smiled gently. “But Mitya won’t agree to that.”

“Yes, but it would be the truth, if he had killed him!” cried Grushenka. “He was mad then, completely mad, and that was my fault, wretch that I am! But of course he didn’t do it, he didn’t do it! And they’re all against him, the whole town. Even Fenya’s testimony went to show he’d done it. And the people at the shop, and that official, and at the tavern earlier, people heard him say it! They’re all, all against him, all shouting against him.”
“Yes, the evidence piles up terribly,” Alyosha remarked grimly.
“And Grigory—Grigory Vassilyevitch—sticks to his story that the door was open. He swears he saw it, and nothing will shake him. I went and talked to him myself. He was rude about it, too.”
“Yes, that may be the strongest evidence against him,” said Alyosha.

“And as for Mitya being mad, he certainly seems so now,” Grushenka began, looking oddly anxious and secretive. “Do you know, Alyosha, I’ve wanted to talk to you about this for ages. I go to see him every day and I’m just amazed by him. Tell me, what do you suppose he’s forever talking about? He goes on and on, and I can’t make anything of it. I thought it was something learned that I was too foolish to follow. Only then he suddenly started on about a babe—some child, that is. ‘Why is the babe poor?’ he said. ‘It’s for that babe that I’m going to Siberia now. I’m not a murderer, but I have to go to Siberia!’ What that meant, what babe, I couldn’t tell you for the life of me. I only cried when he said it, because he said it so sweetly. He cried himself, and I cried too. Then he suddenly kissed me and made the sign of the cross over me. What did it mean, Alyosha? Tell me. What is this babe?”
“It must be Rakitin, who’s been visiting him lately,” Alyosha said, smiling, “though ... this isn’t Rakitin’s doing. I didn’t see Mitya yesterday. I’ll see him today.”

“No, it isn’t Rakitin. It’s his brother, Ivan Fyodorovitch, who’s upsetting him. It’s his visits that do it, that’s what it is,” Grushenka began, and then stopped short. Alyosha stared at her in astonishment.
“Ivan visits him? Has he been there? Mitya told me himself that Ivan hasn’t come once.”

“There ... there! What a girl I am! Letting things slip!” cried Grushenka, flustered, blushing all at once. “Wait, Alyosha, hush! Since I’ve said this much, I’ll tell you the whole truth. He’s been to see him twice. The first time was the moment he arrived. He raced here from Moscow straight away, of course, before I got sick. The second time was a week ago. He told Mitya not to tell you about it, whatever happened, and not to tell anyone at all, really. He came in secret.”
Alyosha sat deep in thought, weighing something. The news had plainly made an impression on him.

“Ivan doesn’t talk to me about Mitya’s case,” he said slowly. “He’s hardly said a word to me these last two months. And every time I go to see him, he seems irritated that I’ve come, so I haven’t been near him for three weeks. H’m!... if he was there a week ago ... then there certainly has been a change in Mitya this week.”

“There has been a change,” Grushenka agreed quickly. “They’ve got a secret, they’ve got a secret! Mitya told me himself that there was a secret, and such a secret that Mitya can’t rest. Before that he was cheerful—and he is cheerful now, for that matter—but when he shakes his head like that, you know, and paces the room and keeps tugging at the hair on his right temple with his right hand, then I know something’s weighing on his mind.... I know! He was cheerful before, though, and he’s cheerful today, too.”
“But you just said he was worried.”

“Yes, he’s worried and cheerful both. One minute he’s irritable, then cheerful, then irritable again. And you know, Alyosha, I’m always amazed at him. With this terrible thing hanging over his head, he sometimes laughs at the most trifling things, like a baby himself.”
“And did he really tell you not to mention Ivan to me? Did he say, ‘Don’t tell him’?”

“Yes, he told me, ‘Don’t tell him.’ It’s you Mitya’s most afraid of. Because it’s a secret, and he said so himself. Alyosha, darling, go to him, find out what their secret is, and come and tell me,” Grushenka begged, suddenly eager. “Set my mind at rest, so I can know the worst that’s coming to me. That’s why I sent for you.”
“You think it concerns you? If it did, he wouldn’t have told you there was a secret.”
“I don’t know. Maybe he wants to tell me and doesn’t dare. He’s giving me a warning. There’s a secret, he says, but he won’t tell me what it is.”
“And what do you think?”

“What do I think? That it’s all over for me, that’s what. The three of them have been plotting to finish me, because Katerina’s part of it. It’s all Katerina, it all comes from her. She’s this and she’s that, which means I’m not. He tells me so in advance, to warn me. He plans to throw me over, that’s the whole secret. They’ve planned it together, the three of them—Mitya, Katerina and Ivan Fyodorovitch. Alyosha, I’ve wanted to ask you for ages. A week ago he suddenly told me that Ivan was in love with Katerina, because he goes to see her so often. Did he tell me the truth or not? Tell me, on your conscience, tell me the worst.”
“I won’t tell you a lie. I don’t think Ivan is in love with Katerina Ivanovna.”

“Oh, that’s what I thought! He’s lying to me, the shameless cheat, that’s all it is! And he was jealous of me just now so that he could put the blame on me afterward. He’s stupid, he can’t hide what he’s up to. He’s so open, you know.... But I’ll pay him back, I’ll pay him back! ‘You believe I did it,’ he said. He said that to me, to me. He threw that in my face! God forgive him! Just wait, I’ll make things hot for Katerina at the trial! I’ll say one little word then ... I’ll tell everything then!”
And she burst into bitter tears again.

“Here’s what I can tell you for certain, Grushenka,” said Alyosha, rising. “First, he loves you. He loves you more than anyone in the world, and you alone, believe me. I know. I do know. Second, I don’t want to pry his secret out of him. But if he tells me of his own accord today, I’ll say straight out that I’ve promised to tell you. Then I’ll come to you today and tell you. Only ... I think ... Katerina Ivanovna has nothing to do with it, and the secret is about something else. That’s certain. It doesn’t seem likely to me that it’s about Katerina Ivanovna. Goodbye for now.”

Alyosha shook her hand. Grushenka was still crying. He could see she put little faith in his comfort, but having had her cry and spoken of her trouble, she was the better for it. He was sorry to leave her in such a state, but he was pressed for time. He still had a great deal to do.
